clinicalPearls: A heterogeneous group of inherited platelet disorders defined by deficient granule content, comprising dense granule (delta), alpha granule (grey platelet syndrome) and combined (alpha-delta) forms.
Patients present with lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding: easy bruising, epistaxis, menorrhagia and prolonged bleeding after surgery or dental extraction.
Platelet count is usually normal, though grey platelet syndrome is characteristically associated with mild thrombocytopenia and large agranular platelets.
Light transmission aggregometry typically shows absent second-wave aggregation and a blunted response to ADP, adrenaline and collagen.
Dense granule deficiency can be confirmed by whole-mount electron microscopy showing reduced granule number or by flow-cytometric mepacrine uptake studies.
Storage pool defects may be isolated or part of syndromes such as Hermansky-Pudlak (with oculocutaneous albinism) and Chediak-Higashi.
Grey platelet syndrome arises from NBEAL2 mutations and may progress to marrow fibrosis and splenomegaly.
Management centres on antifibrinolytics, desmopressin for minor procedures and platelet transfusion for major bleeding, with judicious use given alloimmunisation risk.
reference.pathophysiology: Platelet storage pool disease results from defective formation, cargo loading or retention of platelet secretory granules. Dense (delta) granules normally store ADP, ATP, calcium and serotonin that amplify platelet activation and recruitment; their deficiency impairs the secondary wave of aggregation. Alpha granules store adhesive and haemostatic proteins including von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, factor V and platelet factor 4; their absence, as in grey platelet syndrome from NBEAL2 mutation, produces agranular platelets and can drive marrow fibrosis through unregulated growth-factor release. In syndromic forms such as Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi, mutations in genes governing lysosome-related organelle biogenesis and vesicle trafficking affect melanosomes and granules alike, explaining the associated albinism. The common consequence is impaired granule secretion and a functional platelet defect causing mucocutaneous bleeding despite an often normal platelet count.
additionalDifferentials: Aspirin or other antiplatelet drug effect
Acquired platelet dysfunction from uraemia or myeloproliferative disease
Vascular or connective tissue bleeding disorders
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film for platelet number and morphology
Light transmission platelet aggregometry with multiple agonists
Whole-mount transmission electron microscopy for dense granule count
Flow-cytometric mepacrine uptake and release studies
Platelet nucleotide (ADP/ATP) content and secretion assays
von Willebrand factor antigen and activity to exclude von Willebrand disease
Targeted genetic testing (for example NBEAL2, HPS genes, LYST)
redFlags: Life-threatening haemorrhage after trauma, surgery or childbirth
Progressive splenomegaly and marrow fibrosis in grey platelet syndrome
Pulmonary fibrosis or colitis suggesting underlying Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome
Recurrent severe infections or lymphohistiocytosis suggesting Chediak-Higashi syndrome
reference.prognosis: Bleeding is usually mild to moderate and lifelong, and most patients have a normal life expectancy with appropriate peri-procedural precautions. Prognosis is chiefly determined by any associated syndrome, such as pulmonary fibrosis in Hermansky-Pudlak or the immunodeficiency of Chediak-Higashi.
pitfalls: Attributing mucocutaneous bleeding to a normal platelet count and overlooking a qualitative defect.
Missing an underlying syndrome such as Hermansky-Pudlak by not examining for oculocutaneous albinism.
Interpreting aggregometry without accounting for recent antiplatelet or non-steroidal drug exposure.
Repeated platelet transfusion leading to alloimmunisation and refractoriness.
Failing to give peri-operative antifibrinolytic cover for mucosal surgery.
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood, current edition
International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis guidance on inherited platelet function disorders
management: Antifibrinolytics such as tranexamic acid for mucocutaneous bleeding and dental or surgical cover
Desmopressin (DDAVP) to enhance haemostasis for minor procedures and bleeding episodes
Platelet transfusion reserved for major bleeding or major surgery, minimising alloimmunisation
Avoid antiplatelet drugs including aspirin and NSAIDs that further impair platelet function
Hormonal therapy (combined oral contraceptive or levonorgestrel intrauterine system) with iron replacement for menorrhagia and iron-deficiency anaemia
Genetic counselling and evaluation for associated syndromes such as Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi
Haematology-led peri-procedural planning and surveillance for syndrome-specific complications such as pulmonary fibrosis
